Samsung sees rising chip production requests from BYD, Google, AMD- Nikkei Asia

BYD, Google, AMD, Tesla and others are looking increasingly to Samsung Electronics for contract chipmaking services as surging demand for AI infrastructure strains the advanced chipmaking capacity of market leader TSMC, Nikkei Asia has learned.

Samsung has seen a surge in inquiries from existing and potential global customers, including those in China, looking to use its advanced chip manufacturing capacity, according to six people with knowledge of the matter.

BYD, China's top electric vehicle maker, has been in talks with Samsung about building future generations of autonomous driving chips, while Google is engaging with the South Korean company about potentially producing its next-generation Axion processors, set to launch around 2028, two people familiar with the matter told Nikkei Asia. Google is also considering asking Samsung to build part of its key Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) for AI computing workloads, as early as 2028, one of the people said.

"TSMC is prioritizing advanced-node production not only because it reinforces its tech leadership and long-term strategy, but also because those nodes are more profitable and remain in short supply," said an executive from a Chinese autochip designer, who asked not to be named. "Samsung's yields still lag behind TSMC's, but capacity availability has made it an increasingly attractive option."

Yield is the industry term for production quality, measured as the percentage of chips produced that meet the required specifications and performance.

TSMC, Samsung and Intel are the world's only chipmakers that can offer cutting-edge chip production at a large scale. TSMC has secured the majority of such orders, as well as orders for advanced chip packaging services, from the likes of Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Broadcom, Marvell and MediaTek. These clients take up a large share of the Taiwanese chipmaking group's advanced chipmaking capacity.

Intel, which mainly manufactures chips for in-house use, is working to attract more customers to adopt its advanced chipmaking and packaging capacity.

The Chinese auto industry executive said many chip designers in the country are now pursuing a dual-sourcing strategy, spreading orders between TSMC and Samsung rather than relying on a single foundry, with exact allocation depending on the product.

"Geopolitical factors also push some U.S. clients to use multiple contract chipmakers, if available out there, if they can," another chip industry executive with knowledge told Nikkei Asia.

"TSMC's advanced chip production capacity is really full, which is hard for Chinese clients who have smaller volumes to place new orders, so several have turned to approach Samsung for future possibilities," said an executive-level chip industry source who is familiar with the matter.

Google has been a driving force in the multi-foundry strategy, sources told Nikkei Asia. MediaTek, Taiwan's top chip developer, is helping Google to work with both TSMC and Intel for advanced chip packaging, Nikkei Asia earlier reported, while Qualcomm, the U.S. mobile chip king, has long made use of both TSMC's and Samsung's services.

However, using multiple foundries for advanced chip production requires substantial investment in adapting chip designs to different chipmakers' manufacturing processes, along with greater R&D and supply-chain coordination. Such a strategy is typically viable only for deep-pocketed chip developers, given the additional engineering and workforce costs involved.

Meanwhile, capacity constraints at TSMC are pushing other existing customers to potentially place more orders with Samsung, sources said.

Tesla works with both Samsung and TSMC on various products, including its AI5 chips used in its cars and robots. The upcoming AI6, however, will be made by Samsung in Texas. Tesla founder Elon Musk also announced a partnership with Intel for its future terafab projects in Texas, aiming to bring more critical chip production back to the U.S. and help meet growing demand.

AMD and Nvidia, key clients of TSMC, are also working with Samsung on some chip projects due to capacity constraints. AMD, for example, is in talks to build some future CPUs with Samsung from 2028, one source with knowledge of the situation said.

Nvidia's Groq language processing units (LPUs) are produced by Samsung, and the U.S. chipmaker has not decided whether production of the next generation of these highly specialized chips will be given to other contract chipmakers. The majority of Nvidia's chips are made exclusively by TSMC.

The increasing requests for leading-edge chip production for Samsung would mark a victory for the South Korean chipmaker's foundry business, which used to mainly serve its own consumer electronics and home appliance divisions.

The growing foundry business comes as Samsung is also riding the AI investment boom, enjoying exponentially growing demand for its memory products, including high-bandwidth memory chips, DRAM and NAND flash memories.

Samsung said that it does not comment on customers.

New orders would help Samsung's foundry unit rebound from a recent downturn. The company said earnings for the segment declined in the first quarter due to it being the off-peak season, but it did not elaborate on how big the dip was.

Samsung's foundry and system large-scale integration business units posted a combined 6.9 trillion won ($4.6 billion) in sales in the first quarter, up from 6 trillion won a year ago. Samsung does not break down its earnings for the two units, the latter of which makes an array of logic and analog chips, including image sensors and display chips.

BYD declined to comment. Google said it does not comment on the details of its supply chain.

Exclusive: Apple to Begin Foldable iPhone Mass Production in July, Hinge Problem Resolved

Apple will begin mass production of its first foldable iPhone from late July. While speculation about a launch delay recently emerged due to hinge problems, it has been confirmed that Apple is pushing ahead with a September unveiling as originally planned.

According to reporting by The Elec on the 24th, based on interviews with Apple supply chain sources in Korea and Taiwan, Apple has finalized the major specifications for the foldable iPhone, including the display, case, and mechanical components, and has entered the mass production preparation stage. Foxconn will handle production of the initial volume. A first round of trial production was carried out this past April, and mass production is expected to begin around late July. The September unveiling schedule is also expected to proceed without major issues.

Trial production is the procedure of validating the design, components, assembly process, and quality standards under actual production conditions before a new product enters mass production. It signifies that product development has passed the final validation stage and moved into the mass production preparation stage. For products like the foldable iPhone, which require multiple components such as the panel, hinge, cover glass, and frame to be precisely joined together, trial production results are a key variable for the launch schedule.

The Apple foldable iPhone uses a foldable organic light emitting diode (OLED) panel supplied by Samsung Display, along with the hinge module, cover glass, and mechanical components. Samsung Display recently received approval from Apple for the initial volume of foldable OLED modules from its Vietnam plant. It has completed mass production preparation through the module stage, in which the driver circuit, flexible printed circuit board (FPCB), and protective components are attached to the OLED panel.

The hinge for the foldable iPhone is supplied by Taiwan's Shin Zu Shing and the United States' Amphenol. They supply hinge modules made using a 3D printing method. The hinge determines the opening and closing feel when the screen is folded and unfolded, as well as the crease at the fold and the durability. Since it is a component that does not exist in ordinary bar type smartphones, it determines the level of completion of the foldable product.

It has been reported that there were in fact hinge related problems during the development process. A Taiwan industry source said, "After durability testing at the level of several million cycles, slight noise occurred in the hinge," adding that "in some assembly processes, the tolerances were larger than expected, so the defect rate rose somewhat." The source went on to add that "most of these problems have now been resolved."

Recently, observations have emerged in the industry that the launch of the foldable iPhone could be delayed due to hinge problems. The analysis that Apple could push back the actual sales timing even if it holds the September unveiling event has gained traction. Since it is the first foldable smartphone, Apple may apply strict quality standards at the last moment.

Apple also appears likely to adjust its iPhone launch strategy somewhat. With the addition of the foldable model, the central axis of the September new product unveiling event is expected to shift toward the Pro lineup and the foldable model, and there is a possibility that the standard model will be split off into a separate launch schedule.

An Apple supply chain company source said, "This year the unveiling will center on the Pro, Pro Max, and Ultra (foldable)," adding that "with the addition of the foldable iPhone, among the existing iPhone lineup, the standard model could see its launch pushed back to next spring."

A few thoughts after reading Morgan Stanley’s takeaways from NVIDIA’s NDR:

1. NVIDIA expects the memory shortage to persist for several years.

This is particularly notable coming from NVIDIA—a company that arguably has the best visibility into global AI demand and one of the most sophisticated supply-chain operations in the world.

2. How should we interpret NVIDIA’s comment that shortages in compute, networking, or memory can be mitigated by optimizing the other two?

Could NVIDIA be considering a new architectural approach in which networking is used to compensate for constrained local memory capacity? CXL and memory pooling could potentially be part of the answer.

3. Has NVIDIA’s view of Groq changed?

NVIDIA previously appeared to dismiss Groq’s SRAM-based architecture as suitable only for a niche market. However, its latest comments emphasizing the importance of Groq’s technology suggest that its thinking may be evolving.

4. A more speculative thought: I am increasingly bearish on Apple.

I believe Apple could begin facing significant pressure from 4Q26 onward. Even NVIDIA is struggling with memory bottlenecks. It is difficult to see how Apple can remain unaffected if the shortage becomes more severe.

Apple and the hyperscalers will undoubtedly develop technologies that reduce memory requirements. However, for hyperscalers, any efficiency gains are likely to be absorbed by Jevons’ paradox.

Memory is currently one of the biggest constraints on expanding the supply of compute, the most valuable resource in the AI economy. Therefore, when hyperscalers reduce the amount of memory required per unit of compute, the rational response is not to purchase less memory. It is to deploy more compute and reinvest the saved resources into buying even more memory.

This dynamic could continue driving memory demand from the AI server market higher, while squeezing consumer-device companies such as Apple that must compete for the same scarce memory supply without enjoying the same AI-driven economics.

Under such a scenario, I would not be surprised to see the price of an iPhone increase by as much as $400.

不要纠结文内一部分事实错误，我只想分享这篇内容的核心

市场真正交易的不是当下利润，而是利润能否持续；当牛鞭效应推动价格和订单被层层放大时，最好的财报往往意味着周期最接近拐点。

————————————

“鞭子的末梢，从来不知道鞭柄在做什么。

你站在鞭子的末梢，感受到的是音爆，是撕裂空气的速度，是那种被巨力裹挟着、身不由己的飞舞。

你以为自己在飞。你确实在飞。

但你不是在飞，你是在被甩。鞭柄只是轻轻抖了一下，手腕移动了十厘米。

你移动了三米，然后撞在墙上，断成两截。半导体行业就是这根鞭子。

在1996年的一个午后，一个惠普的采购经理在咖啡机前站了很久。

他盯着杯子里旋转的黑色液体，做了一个决定：多订30%的内存。不是因为订单增加了30%，而是因为万一明年缺货，他就是罪人。

他不确定未来会怎样。他唯一确定的是，如果别人都订了、他没订，那他就完蛋了。

他签下订单的那个瞬间，鞭柄动了一下。十二个月后，内存价格崩塌，全行业亏损数十亿美元。

那个采购经理，已经换了一份工作，在一家汽车零部件公司做供应链总监。没有人记得他。

但他是那场地震的第一块多米诺骨牌。这就是牛鞭效应。

它有一个更学术的名字，叫“长鞭效应”，或者“需求变异放大效应”。

用任何一个名字称呼它，它都是一样的东西：在一条供应链里，终端需求的微小波动，在向上游传导的过程中，被每一层逐级放大，最终在源头形成剧烈的震荡。

你不需要是一个经济学家才能理解它。你只需要想象一条鞭子：鞭柄移动十厘米，鞭梢移动好几米。

终端消费者的需求变动十厘米，存储芯片的价格变动好几米。不是线性关系，是杠杆关系。这条鞭子有几节。

第一节，是消费者。他们多买了几部手机，因为经济不错，因为年终奖发得比去年多一点。

他们不知道自己的购买行为会引发什么。他们只是想要一部新手机。

第二节，是零售商。他们发现库存消耗得比预期快，于是向经销商多下了订单。不仅要补足库存，还要为未来的增长预留缓冲。

第三节，是经销商。他们收到的订单增加了，于是向整机厂发出了更大的订单。他们开始担心：如果供货跟不上，客户就会去找别人。

第四节，是整机厂。他们看着堆在桌上的采购申请，做了一道简单的数学题：当前需求加上安全库存，再加上对未来的乐观预期，等于一个被放大了30%的数字。

第五节，是芯片设计公司。他们收到的订单已经面目全非，终端消费者的那一点点增加，在这里变成了庞大的、不容置疑的需求信号。他们必须抢产能，必须提前锁定供应，必须再多订40%。

第六节，是存储原厂——三星、海力士、美光。他们看着涌入的订单，发现供不应求。于是他们涨价。

涨价的消息顺着鞭子传回下游，下游恐慌了：现在不买，以后更贵。于是他们更疯狂地囤货。囤货制造了更多的“需求”，更多的“需求”推动更多的涨价。

这就是牛市。所有人的订单都建立在别人放大的预期之上，每一层都在为上一层虚构的需求买单，每一个人都以为自己是在为真实需求备货。实际上，他们是在为自己的恐惧备货。

但鞭子可以向上甩，也可以向下甩。当终端消费者的购买量只是轻微下滑——经济有一点疲软，手机少卖了几百万部——零售商发现，仓库里的货比预期多。

他们暂停下单，先消化库存。这个微小的停顿，传到经销商，订单减少。传到整机厂，订单取消。

传到芯片设计公司，订单归零。传到存储原厂，订单变成负数。原厂还在拼命生产——因为产线不能停，因为晶圆厂从投产到量产需要几个月——但仓库已经堆满了没人要的芯片。然后价格崩塌。

所有之前被放大了无数倍的虚假需求，在一瞬间消失。整个产业链开始漫长的去库存周期。

在这个周期里，那些曾经把利润推上巅峰的涨价，会反过来把利润推下深渊。

这就是半导体周期。它不是偶尔崩盘，它必然崩盘。它的崩盘不是基本面出了问题，恰恰相反——它的崩盘，是在基本面最完美的时候，突然降临的。

因为最完美的财报，意味着涨价已经到了极限，囤货已经到了极限，那个推动一切往上走的虚假需求，已经到了极限。
2026年7月7日，韩国首尔，汝矣岛。三星电子刚刚发布了人类历史上最炸裂的季度业绩预报：营业利润89.4万亿韩元，约合584亿美元，同比增长1810%。

这个数字超过了英伟达，超过了地球上任何一家公司单季赚钱的纪录。

半导体事业部负责人放话：“今年的营业利润将超过半导体事业开展40年来的累计利润。”两个小时后，股价暴跌近8%，触发熔断。

两周前，同样的剧本在太平洋对岸上演。美光科技交出了史上最强财报——营收414.6亿美元，净利润282.4亿美元，同比暴增1398%。毛利率84.9%，营业利润率81.2%。每一个数字都在证明，存储行业的黄金时代已经降临。第二天，股价暴跌10%。

再往前好多天，闪迪的财报同样炸裂。花旗昨天将目标价从1200美元上调至2200美元，高盛同步跟进。散户们看到“翻倍”两个字，冲了进去。然后，闪迪也崩了。

从6月19日到7月7日，不到三周。韩国KOSPI指数从9300点跌至7656点，跌掉了整个上半年涨幅的近三分之一。三星电子从374000韩元跌至293500韩元，跌幅21.5%。SK海力士从2980000韩元跌至2200000韩元，跌幅26.2%。美光从1250美元跌至944美元，跌幅24.5%。

这些下跌，发生在一个没有任何实质性利空的背景里。没有战争，没有金融危机，没有贸易制裁。多头们找不到凶手。
他们先是怪Meta——Meta说了一句“未来或许会出售算力”，一句棉花糖似的、它自己都不确定是什么意思的话。然后怪苹果——苹果把Mac和iPad涨价了，他们说这是苹果在压榨供应商。

最后怪三星的营收不及“最乐观预期”——1810%的利润增长，因为营收比那个从来没人确认过的“最乐观数字”低了1.7%，就成了利空。

这不是分析，这是在尸检报告上编造死因。一具尸体躺在那里，胸口插着一把刀，法医却指着尸体脚趾上的一块淤青说：看，这就是致死原因。

Meta的算力、苹果的涨价、1.7%的营收偏差——这些不是刀，这些是淤青。真正的刀，插在更深处。它叫牛鞭效应。

市场在怀疑的，不是这份财报的真实性，而是这份利润的可持续性。利润从哪里来？从涨价来。美光的产量在2026年基本持平，全球DRAM产能只增长了5%。

三星也一样。那1810%的利润增长，1388%的利润增长，来自哪里？来自价格标签被不断往上贴。在过去几个季度里，DRAM价格暴涨了超过100%。

但涨价的速度正在坍塌——从50%降到40%，从40%降到20%。

产能已经定死，出货量不可能暴增，利润增长就只取决于涨价速度。涨价速度在崩塌，利润的加速度就在崩塌。市场问的不是“这个季度赚了多少”，而是“下个季度还能赚更多吗”。

如果涨价从50%降到20%，利润增速就会从爆炸变成普通。如果涨价停止，利润就会停止增长。如果涨价逆转——那一天总是会来的，因为牛鞭效应的鞭梢已经开始往回甩了——利润就会雪崩。

到那时，美光的10倍PE会在瞬间变成50倍、100倍，不是股价涨了，是利润没了。那10倍PE，不是在说“这家公司很便宜”，它是在说“我不相信你明年还能赚这么多钱”。这是市场对周期性盈利的死刑判决。

但多头们有一个信仰。他们说，存储不是商品，存储是AI时代的必需品。所以它可以永远涨价，永远稀缺，永远被需要。但必需品，恰恰是最不能无限涨价的东西。粮食，是这个星球上最无可辩驳的必需品。

一个人可以不买手机，不买电脑，不碰任何电子产品，但他不能不吃粮食。但粮食能一直涨价吗？不能。当粮食涨到买不起的时候，人会饿死。

Article Summary:

- ASML is considering raising the prices of its EUV systems, citing surging demand from the AI and memory semiconductor markets. It has also notified some customers that it plans to increase DUV equipment prices by 10%.
- TSMC, ASML’s largest customer, is pushing back against price increases for both EUV and DUV systems. However, some Chinese semiconductor companies have accepted the higher DUV prices.
- ASML has raised its 2026 revenue outlook to €43 billion–€45 billion and plans to increase annual production capacity for two of its key systems by 30% this year.
- TSMC faces a dilemma: ASML’s equipment is essential for expanding its AI chip and advanced CoWoS packaging capacity, but the company also wants to keep costs under control while securing additional systems.
- China is likely to be hit hardest by the DUV price increases because export restrictions prevent Chinese companies from purchasing EUV systems and certain advanced DUV systems, while alternative suppliers remain limited.

Jukan’s Take:

TEL and other equipment makers are already pursuing aggressive price increases. In meetings with the media and sell-side analysts, TEL said it is seeking to raise equipment prices by as much as 50% over the long term.

Still, it is somewhat surprising that TSMC is already pushing back. TSMC appears to be extremely focused on protecting its margins.

- Apple is actively searching for acquisition targets, including semiconductor startups, to strengthen its in-house AI server chip capabilities.
- Its current M2 Ultra-based servers have limitations when processing large AI models, forcing Apple to run some features of the new Siri on Nvidia chips hosted in Google Cloud.
- Delays to Apple’s next-generation AI server chip, “Baltra,” have also fueled concerns that the company’s semiconductor design expertise remains too heavily focused on mobile applications.
- Apple is seeking to reduce its dependence on Nvidia through M5 and M7 Ultra-based server chips and a joint development project with Broadcom. However, the M7 Ultra-based product is not expected until 2029.
- Given Apple’s recent consideration of major acquisitions, potential changes to its cash policy, and an eventual CEO transition, the company may be more willing than in the past to pursue a large-scale acquisition of a semiconductor or AI company.

The delay to Baltra, combined with Apple’s search for semiconductor startup acquisitions, raises the question of whether Apple is effectively admitting that it lacks sufficient expertise in server chips.

The Ohio semiconductor campus drew attention as Intel’s first new manufacturing site in 40 years. Under the first phase of the project, Intel said it would invest approximately $28 billion, or about 41.2 trillion won, to complete two next-generation semiconductor plants—Fab 27 and Fab 28—by 2025. The company also planned to hire 3,000 engineers and manufacture cutting-edge chips there. Then-U.S. President Joe Biden attended the groundbreaking ceremony in September 2022, where he highlighted the significance of the CHIPS Act and reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to strengthening the semiconductor industry.

However, major U.S. technology companies such as Nvidia, Apple, and AMD have relied on Taiwan’s TSMC for contract chip manufacturing, leaving Intel Foundry struggling to secure customers. As its financial difficulties continued, Intel announced large-scale workforce reductions and investment cuts last year and postponed the start of operations at the Ohio plants until 2030 or 2031.

The potential “megadeal” reflects an alignment of interests between SK Hynix and Intel. The Trump administration has been urging Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix to expand their investments in the United States as it seeks to reorganize the semiconductor supply chain around domestic production.

Samsung Electronics is investing approximately $37 billion, or about 54.46 trillion won, to build an advanced foundry plant and research and development facilities in Taylor, Texas, with operations scheduled to begin next year. SK Hynix, meanwhile, is investing approximately $3.87 billion, or about 5.69 trillion won, in an advanced packaging facility for high-bandwidth memory in Indiana, which is targeted to begin operations in 2028.

Pressure from the U.S. government for additional investment, however, remains ongoing. Speaking at an event at Micron’s New York plant on the 10th local time, U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said, “I want to bring Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix to the United States and have them build manufacturing facilities here.”

The semiconductor industry has interpreted Lutnick’s remarks as a demand for the companies to establish not only foundry and packaging facilities in the United States, but also front-end memory production facilities for products such as DRAM. Kim Dae-jong, a professor at Sejong University’s School of Business, said, “The United States is seeking to establish a fully integrated artificial intelligence semiconductor supply chain encompassing design, foundry production, memory, and packaging—all within its own borders.”

In a related development, SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won said at the Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry’s Summer Forum in Jeju on the 15th, “Memory chip prices are currently abnormally high. We need to increase supply to bring prices down.”

“We need to build semiconductor plants not only in the Honam region but also in the United States,” Chey added. “We are currently looking for a site. We need to build quickly.”

Intel, for its part, would be able to secure liquidity by selling the Ohio campus, which had become a costly burden, giving it a foundation from which to restructure its foundry business. Intel’s foundry division posted a loss of $2.2 billion last year and recorded another $2.4 billion loss in the first quarter of this year.

Intel recently recruited former SK Hynix CEO Lee Seok-hee as executive vice president in charge of its foundry division and is focusing on strengthening its back-end capabilities, including improving production yields.
